purpose: How a website-and-hosting reseller designs a fixed-scope site-build-plus-care-plan offer for one chosen local niche, prices both revenue legs from a documented cost floor instead of invented market rates, wins founding clients and compounds a referral loop, and scopes and positions every deal so honestly that scope creep, outcome-guarantee demands, and asset lock-in never enter the client book.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors
the operator is a solo or very small website-and-hosting reseller serving local small businesses, with capacity measured in build slots per month rather than teams
revenue is a one-time site-build fee plus a monthly care plan (hosting custody, updates, backups, a small edit allowance), and both legs are presented together at proposal time
all pricing content is mechanism and tier logic only; actual amounts are derived by the operator from their own documented costs, labor hours, and local quote checks
contract, consumer-protection, and cooling-off obligations vary by jurisdiction; this KB names the obligation class and defers specifics to current local rules
exclusions: choosing the build stack and running the standardized build pipeline (content intake mechanics, design system, build, review, launch), the quality/performance/accessibility baseline, domain/DNS/email cutover, and the launch checklist — that is the site build & delivery KB

hosting architecture for the site portfolio, backup/update/security operations, care-plan tier operations, monthly value reporting, and retention/reactivation/offboarding with asset handover — that is the hosting & retention KB
any invented market rate or specific dollar figure for build fees or care plans stated as fact — prices appear only as derivation mechanisms and qualitative tiers
SEO, traffic, ranking, or revenue guarantees, and any performance claim that cannot be verified by measurement
retention through hostage-holding of the client's domain, content, or credentials — the client owns their assets and lock-in comes only from service quality
personalized legal, tax, or financial advice — contract and consumer-protection points are named as obligation classes to verify in the operator's jurisdiction

competency_questions.question: What exactly does a client buy from this business — what is the unit of sale, what does the build fee cover, and what does the monthly plan cover?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OFFER_THESIS states the package as the unit of sale with both revenue legs, and PACKAGE_ARCHITECTURE enumerates the deliverables and exclusions the build fee buys

competency_questions.question: Which local niche should the offer be built for, and by what criteria is a niche judged worth productizing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NICHE_SELECTION gives the scorecard criteria (recurring ability to pay, urgency of presence, content simplicity, referral density, low custom-feature demand) and a way to verify them against a counted local sample

competency_questions.question: Who actually signs the contract in this niche, what do they fear, and how must that shape the language of the offer and the sales conversation?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BUYER_REALITY profiles the time-poor, non-technical, often-burned owner-operator and translates each fear into a specific offer or conversation choice

competency_questions.question: How are the build fee and the monthly plan price derived without inventing market rates?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRICING_MECHANISM derives both prices from a documented cost floor (tool and hosting costs, labor hours, expected support minutes) plus a margin target and local quote checks, with no fabricated figure stated as fact

competency_questions.question: Which claims about what a website will do for a business are honest, which are banned, and how is a claim tested for verifiability?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HONEST_CAPABILITY_POSITIONING separates what a site can do (credibility, converting existing demand) from what it cannot (conjure demand, guarantee rankings) and states the verifiability test every public claim must pass

competency_questions.question: How does the offer guarantee the client's ownership of their domain and content while still selling bundled hosting custody?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ASSET_OWNERSHIP_PROMISE states the ownership and exit terms (domain in the client's name or transferable on request, content owned by the client, a stated handover path), and CARE_PLAN_OFFER_FRAMING shows the plan surviving the client's right to leave

competency_questions.question: How does the operator win the first handful of paying clients before any portfolio exists?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OUTBOUND_FIRST_CLIENTS gives the cold-start path: warm introductions first, visibly absent or broken sites in the niche approached without fear tactics, and a disclosed founding-client rate traded for testimonial permission at signing

competency_questions.question: How do finished sites turn into a compounding referral loop and partner channel that keeps the pipeline full?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PROOF_PORTFOLIO defines the verifiable proof kit, REFERRAL_LOOP the ask timing and disclosed thanks mechanics, LOCAL_PARTNER_CHANNELS the adjacent-professional arrangements, and PIPELINE_CADENCE the source-tracked follow-up and capacity-aware intake

competency_questions.question: How is a prospect qualified, and which findings must disqualify a deal before any quote is issued?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DISCOVERY_QUALIFICATION lists the discovery questions (goal, domain control, content readiness, budget class, decision-maker present) and the explicit disqualifiers (needs beyond the package, guarantee demands, no path to domain control)

competency_questions.question: What must the written scope contain so that scope creep dies at the change-order gate instead of eroding the build?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SCOPE_AGREEMENT enumerates deliverables, exclusions, revision counts, client obligations and the change-order path, and SCOPE_CREEP_DEFENSE routes every out-of-scope request to that path or the parking lot

competency_questions.question: Who is responsible for producing the site's content, and what happens to the timeline and the deal when the client stalls?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CONTENT_RESPONSIBILITY_SPLIT fixes the responsibility model (client-provided with dates, priced done-for-you, or draft-first) with a written stall consequence, and EXPECTATION_SETTING carries that consequence into the client-facing timeline

competency_questions.question: What are the ethical-selling rules of this trade, especially toward non-technical and vulnerable buyers?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ETHICAL_SELLING_GUARDRAILS states disclosure-first total-cost transparency, the ban on fear-selling, concrete vulnerable-buyer care steps, and disclosed referral incentives, flagging cooling-off obligations as jurisdiction-dependent

competency_questions.question: What does 'sold correctly' mean — what must exist before a signed deal may pass to the build process and the hosting book?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PROPOSAL_AND_CLOSE defines the proposal artifact with first-year total cost and the ownership statement attached, and SALE_TO_DELIVERY_HANDOFF lists the definition-of-sold checklist the handoff packet must satisfy

competency_questions.question: How do the offer's unit economics work — what makes the recurring leg compound, and what breaks the model?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OFFER_ECONOMICS_MODEL explains build-fee versus recurring-base mechanics, monthly capacity math, and the failure conditions (underpriced care plan, churn outpacing new plans) as mechanisms computed from the operator's own numbers

glossary.definition: A service sold as if it were a product: fixed deliverables, fixed price, fixed process, repeated identically deal after deal — the opposite of bespoke agency work estimated per project.
The recurring monthly plan sold with the build: hosting custody, software updates, backups, and a small content-edit allowance, with a stated response class; the second and compounding revenue leg.
The gradual expansion of a fixed-scope project through small unpriced requests ('while you're in there…') that individually feel too petty to refuse and collectively consume the margin of the build.
A written, separately priced addition to an already-signed scope; the single legitimate path by which new work enters a fixed-scope deal.
A reduced early rate offered to the first clients, explicitly disclosed as a time-boxed founding arrangement and traded for testimonial and portfolio permission — never disguised as the normal price.

The structured qualification conversation held before any quote, covering the business goal, current domain and site state, who controls the domain, content readiness, budget class, and whether the decision-maker is present.

The engineered cycle in which satisfied clients and adjacent local professionals keep producing warm leads: proof earns the ask, the ask is timed to satisfaction peaks, thanks are disclosed, and every lead's source is tracked.
The abusive practice of keeping a client's domain, content, or credentials under the vendor's control so leaving becomes painful; the retention tactic this business categorically bans.

The documented per-deal minimum below which a price loses money: hosting and tool costs per site, expected labor hours at a target effective rate, and the support minutes a plan realistically consumes each month.

The checklist a signed deal must satisfy before delivery begins: scope signed, deposit received, content plan dated, domain-control status verified, expectations acknowledged, and the care-plan tier recorded.

nodes.definition: Fix what is actually for sale before anything else: a fixed-scope website build for one kind of local business plus a monthly care plan (hosting custody, software updates, backups, and a small edit allowance) presented together as one productized package. The unit of sale is the package, not hours — the build fee prices the sprint that gets a correct site live, and the care plan prices the ongoing custody of a working site. This thesis commits the operator to repeatability: the same deliverables, the same process, the same promises on every deal, so that every later choice — niche, package detail, price, pitch — serves one repeatable offer instead of drifting back into bespoke agency work.

included: the package as the unit of sale
both revenue legs named at proposal time

pros.claim: One repeatable package turns every sale into practice on the same deliverable instead of a fresh estimate
pros.example: quoting a landscaper and a bakery from the same five-page package sheet rather than writing two bespoke proposals

cons.claim: Productization deliberately turns away profitable bespoke work that does not fit the package
cons.example: declining a paying booking-system project because the offer sells brochure sites with a contact form

failure_modes: selling hours under a package label so every deal quietly becomes bespoke again
defining the thesis around the operator's favorite technology instead of what the chosen niche actually buys
acceptance_tests: the offer fits on one page stating the deliverable set, both revenue legs, and who it is for, and two readers unfamiliar with the business describe the same product back
revisit_triggers: half of recent deals needed custom exceptions to close
most buyers decline the care-plan leg at proposal

base.update_signal: close rates or exception counts show the packaged offer is not what the niche buys

nodes.definition: Choose one local niche the package is built for, using a scorecard rather than taste: recurring ability to pay (stable-revenue trades such as contractors, clinics, or repair shops that can carry a monthly plan), urgency of web presence (their customers compare providers online before calling), content simplicity (a short stable service list, no catalog churn), referral density (owners in the niche actually talk to each other through supplier counters, trade associations, or shared bookkeepers), and low custom-feature demand (no marketplaces, portals, or inventory systems). Each criterion is checked against a counted sample of the local service area — how many such businesses exist within driving distance and how many have absent, broken, or embarrassing sites — so the choice rests on observed supply, not a hunch.

included: the decision to decline off-niche work
excluded: any claim about a niche's average budgets stated as fact

pros.claim: A niche chosen for referral density makes every finished site advertise to the next buyer
pros.example: three plumbing companies that share a supply house hearing about the same finished plumber site within a month

cons.claim: Committing to one niche concentrates risk in that niche's economy and seasonality
cons.example: a book of landscaper clients going quiet together in the off-season

failure_modes: picking a niche the operator finds glamorous but whose owners feel no urgency about their web presence
scoring the niche on national impressions instead of counting the actual local service area
acceptance_tests: the chosen niche passes all five scorecard criteria with a counted local sample recorded for the urgency and supply checks
revisit_triggers: pipeline data shows off-niche leads converting better than in-niche ones
the local sample shrinks or saturates so few unserved businesses remain

base.update_signal: conversion and referral data from the pipeline re-scores the chosen niche against alternatives

nodes.definition: Understand the person who actually signs: a time-poor owner-operator who answers the phone on a job site, is not technical, and has often been burned before — by a cousin's abandoned half-site, an agency retainer that produced invoices but no visible change, or a vendor who vanished with the domain login. This buyer purchases trust and local proof, not feature lists; their unspoken fears are looking foolish, paying for things they cannot see, and being trapped. Every offer artifact answers those fears directly: plain language with no jargon, the whole price visible in one glance including the first-year total, a you-own-your-stuff promise stated up front, and proof from businesses like theirs rather than design awards.

included: the buyer profile and fear inventory
translation of each fear into offer and conversation choices
excluded: psychological manipulation techniques of any kind

pros.claim: Selling against the buyer's real fears converts trust-damaged prospects competitors cannot reach
pros.example: a roofer who refused three agencies signing because the proposal opened with the domain-stays-yours clause

cons.claim: A fear-informed pitch drifts into fear-selling if the fears are amplified instead of answered
cons.example: the line 'most owners get trapped by their web guy' shifting from empathy to scare tactic in one word choice

failure_modes: writing offer copy for a design-literate audience the niche does not contain
assuming the spouse or office manager who answered the email is the decision-maker
acceptance_tests: every named buyer fear maps to a specific line in the offer or proposal that answers it
revisit_triggers: discovery calls surface an objection the fear inventory does not cover
a generational shift in the niche changes who signs and what they fear

base.update_signal: recurring objections in discovery calls contradict the assumed fear inventory

nodes.definition: Draw the honest line on what a website can and cannot do for a small business, and hold every sales sentence to it. A site can make the business credible when a ready-to-buy searcher compares providers, convert existing demand into calls and form submissions, keep hours and services correct everywhere, and give later marketing a foundation. A site cannot conjure demand that does not exist, and nobody can promise rankings, traffic volumes, or revenue. The operating rule is a verifiability test: a claim may be made only if the operator can name the measurement that would prove or disprove it — load time and uptime are measurable, 'more customers' is not promisable — and a maintained banned-claims list (first-page guarantees, traffic projections, revenue outcomes) keeps forbidden lines out of every pitch, proposal, and portfolio caption.

excluded: how performance is actually measured and reported — delivery and hosting territory

pros.claim: Refusing outcome guarantees filters for clients who stay, because nothing impossible was promised
pros.example: an electrician renewing the plan for a third year because the site does exactly what the pitch said and nothing was owed beyond it

cons.claim: Honest positioning loses deals to competitors who happily guarantee first-page rankings
cons.example: a prospect choosing the vendor who promised to 'get you to number one on Google' within a month

failure_modes: letting one 'you will definitely get more calls' slip into a pitch and creating an unpayable debt
overcorrecting into such modest claims that the offer sounds pointless
acceptance_tests: every claim in the current pitch, proposal template, and proof kit either names its verification method or is deleted
the banned-claims list exists, is dated, and includes ranking, traffic, and revenue guarantees
revisit_triggers: a client repeats a promise back that was never intended as one
a new sales artifact is drafted and has not passed the verifiability test

base.update_signal: a complaint, dispute, or refund request traces back to a claim a client heard as a guarantee

nodes.definition: Bind every acquisition and closing behavior to explicit ethical rules. Disclosure first: the recurring cost is presented as a first-year total alongside the build fee, term and cancellation mechanics are stated in plain words, and any referral incentive behind an introduction is disclosed to the person referred. No fear-selling: outreach may point out that a site is down, broken, or absent as observable fact, but never manufactures dread — no 'you're invisible without us', no invented hack threats, no urgency countdowns. Vulnerable-buyer care: when a buyer is elderly, non-native in the contract language, or visibly confused about recurring billing, the close slows down — restate the total cost plainly, invite a family member or bookkeeper into the decision, and honor any cooling-off or doorstep-sales obligation class that applies, verifying current rules in the operator's jurisdiction.

excluded: jurisdiction-specific consumer-law text — named as an obligation class to verify locally

pros.claim: Disclosure-first selling produces clients who never feel ambushed by the recurring charge
pros.example: zero billing disputes in a book where every proposal showed the first-year total before signature

cons.claim: Slowing a close for a confused buyer sometimes loses the sale to a faster, pushier vendor
cons.example: a shop owner signing that afternoon with a cold-caller while the operator waited for the owner's son to join a second call

failure_modes: outreach templates drifting into scare framing as they get 'optimized' for response rate
an undisclosed partner kickback surfacing later and poisoning both relationships
acceptance_tests: the selling rules are written and dated, and every outreach template and proposal in use passes them on review
any referral arrangement in force is documented as disclosed to the referred party
revisit_triggers: a new outreach channel or script is introduced
a buyer interaction reveals a vulnerability situation the procedure does not cover

base.update_signal: a complaint, regulator inquiry, or partner dispute exposes a gap in the selling rules

nodes.definition: Make client ownership of their assets a structural promise, not a courtesy. The domain is registered in the client's own registrar account from the start, or held under a documented arrangement that transfers it on request without fee or friction; the content, imagery, and the site deliverables produced for the client belong to the client per the contract; credentials the client should hold are handed over at launch rather than hoarded. The exit path is written before the first proposal goes out: what a departing client receives, in what form, and within what stated timeframe class. Retention is earned by service quality alone — the moment leaving is made technically or contractually painful, the business has crossed into hostage-holding, which this offer categorically bans.

excluded: registrar and DNS mechanics of transfers — delivery territory
the offboarding operations checklist — hosting-book territory

pros.claim: A written exit path converts the buyer's biggest fear into a selling point
pros.example: a twice-burned dentist signing specifically because the proposal spelled out what she would receive if she ever left

cons.claim: Genuine portability makes leaving easy, so weak service loses clients faster
cons.example: a client walking to a cheaper host in an afternoon because nothing technical held them

failure_modes: registering client domains under the operator's personal account 'for convenience' and creating accidental hostage-holding
promising ownership verbally while the signed contract stays silent on the exit path
acceptance_tests: every active client's domain is verifiably in their own name or covered by the documented transfer-on-request arrangement
the ownership and exit statement appears in the current proposal template
revisit_triggers: a departing client reports friction reclaiming any asset
a registrar, contract, or policy change alters how the ownership arrangement works

base.update_signal: an exit event or registrar change tests whether the promise holds in practice

nodes.definition: Design the build package as an enumerated, closed list: a page-count band suited to the niche (home, services, about, proof, contact is the classic small-trade shape), one design direction with a fixed number of revision rounds, a contact form that reliably reaches the owner, mobile-correct layout, and consistent business details ready for local listings. Just as important is the enumerated exclusion list — e-commerce, booking engines, membership areas, logo design, copywriting beyond the included allowance — and a short menu of named add-ons, each with its own fixed scope and price mechanism, so that common extras have a legitimate door instead of leaking in free. If tiers exist (a starter and a standard), each tier is itself a closed list; a tier that says 'custom' has stopped being a product.

excluded: how the deliverables are technically built

pros.claim: An enumerated exclusion list settles most scope arguments before they start
pros.example: pointing to the 'booking systems: not included' line when a salon asks for one in week two

cons.claim: A closed list can miss the one deliverable the niche genuinely expects
cons.example: a restaurant package without a menu-update mechanism forcing awkward change orders on day one

failure_modes: writing the inclusions carefully but leaving exclusions implicit, so every gap becomes a negotiation
adding a quiet exception for one client that silently becomes the new package
acceptance_tests: the package sheet enumerates deliverables, exclusions, revision counts, and add-ons, and a stranger can price-relevant-classify any plausible request as included, add-on, or excluded
revisit_triggers: the same change-order request appears across three or more clients
the niche's baseline expectation shifts (a new must-have feature becomes standard)

base.update_signal: clustered change orders or lost deals show the deliverable list no longer matches what the niche buys

nodes.definition: Frame the care plan as it is sold, because the monthly fee is a promise made at proposal time: custody of a working site (hosting arranged and watched), software kept updated, backups kept and restorable, a small monthly edit allowance with a stated response class, and a named person to call when something breaks. Tiers, if offered, differ by edit allowance and response class — mechanisms, never invented market rates. Two framing rules are non-negotiable: the plan's protective core (hosting, updates, backups) is sold as one unsplittable unit because unbundling it creates uninsurable half-clients, and the plan is presented alongside the exit path so the client sees that staying is a monthly choice, not a trap. What the plan operationally involves month to month belongs to the hosting book, not here.

included: the sold promise of the plan
tier logic by allowance and response class

pros.claim: Selling the plan with the build normalizes the recurring fee as part of owning a site
pros.example: a contractor accepting the monthly plan without negotiation because it appeared in the very first quote next to the build fee

cons.claim: A plan promised vaguely at sale time becomes a bag of unpaid expectations later
cons.example: 'we handle updates' heard as 'redesign my homepage whenever I ask' by month four

failure_modes: letting a prospect unbundle backups out of the plan to shave the price, creating an unprotected site with the operator's name on it
promising a response class the solo operator cannot keep across a growing book
acceptance_tests: the plan sheet states custody, updates, backups, the edit allowance, and the response class in plain words, and marks the protective core as one unit
revisit_triggers: support minutes consumed per client drift far from what the framing assumed
clients repeatedly ask at sale time for something no tier contains

base.update_signal: plan-refusal rates at proposal or post-sale expectation disputes show the framing is wrong

nodes.definition: Derive both prices from a documented cost floor instead of copying or inventing market rates. For the build fee: the hours a package build actually takes (measured after the first few, estimated honestly before), multiplied by a target effective rate, plus per-project tool and license costs, plus a margin that funds sales time and rework risk. For the monthly plan: per-site hosting and tool cost, the support minutes a typical client actually consumes, backup storage, and the amortized time of updates, again with margin. Local quote checks — what real competing proposals in the area asked, learned from prospects who share them — sanity-check the result without becoming its source. Prices are versioned: changes apply to new deals, and existing clients are treated per the terms they signed, with any increase communicated by mechanism (notice period, effective date), never by surprise.

excluded: any specific dollar amount asserted as the market rate

pros.claim: A documented floor makes discount pressure a calculation instead of a nerve contest
pros.example: declining a haggled deal in one minute because the asked price sat below the worksheet's floor line

cons.claim: Cost-plus logic can leave value on the table for a niche that would happily pay more
cons.example: underpricing sites for a high-ticket trade because the worksheet only saw hours, not what a single new customer is worth to the client

failure_modes: guessing the monthly support minutes optimistically so every plan quietly loses money
matching a competitor's number without knowing whether it covers anyone's floor
acceptance_tests: a written cost-floor worksheet exists for both legs and both current prices sit above it by the stated margin
the price sheet carries a version and date, and no sales artifact states an invented figure as a market fact
revisit_triggers: measured build hours or support minutes diverge from the worksheet's assumptions
tool, license, or hosting costs change

base.update_signal: tracked hours, support minutes, or input costs contradict the worksheet the prices stand on

nodes.definition: Model how the two legs interact so decisions about mix, capacity, and discounting are made on mechanism rather than mood. Each build adds one monthly plan to the base; the base compounds because plans stack while build fees do not repeat, so after enough accumulated plans the recurring leg covers the operator's fixed costs and the model's break-even month count — computed from the operator's own price sheet and cost floor, never stated as a universal figure — keeps shrinking. Capacity math bounds the intake side: build slots per month at sustainable hours, minus the support load the existing book already consumes, which itself grows with every sale. The model exposes the classic failure: an underpriced care plan feels harmless per client and quietly turns the whole compounding leg into stacked losses, while churn outpacing new plans hollows the base no build volume can refill.

included: break-even framing from the operator's own numbers
excluded: retention operations that protect the base
any asserted industry-average revenue or churn figure

pros.claim: Seeing the recurring base as the real asset stops the operator from optimizing build fees at the plan's expense
pros.example: accepting a modest build margin on a solid client because the plan attached is what the model actually values

cons.claim: A spreadsheet model built on optimistic inputs lends false confidence to bad prices
cons.example: a projection that assumed every client stays for years masking that early churn erases the acquisition cost

failure_modes: counting the recurring base's growth while ignoring the support hours that grow with it
treating projected plan revenue as spendable before the plans have survived their first renewals
acceptance_tests: the model recomputes from the current price sheet and cost floor, and shows the support-load ceiling alongside build capacity
revisit_triggers: actual churn, support load, or build throughput diverges from the model's inputs
a price-sheet version change invalidates the current computation

base.update_signal: observed churn, support minutes, or throughput replace the model's estimated inputs

nodes.definition: Win the first handful of paying clients before any portfolio exists. Order of attack: warm paths first — people who already know the operator (a former employer, the family plumber, the gym owner) convert on trust the cold market will not extend yet; then direct outreach inside the niche to businesses whose web presence is visibly absent, broken, or years out of date, approached with observable fact ('your site shows your old address and does not load on a phone') rather than manufactured dread. The founding-client arrangement makes the missing portfolio explicit: a reduced rate disclosed as a time-boxed founding rate — never passed off as the normal price — traded for a testimonial and portfolio permission collected at signing, plus tolerance for a process still being polished. Five finished founding sites end the cold-start phase and become the proof the next tier of clients buys on.

included: fact-based outreach to visibly broken presences
excluded: the referral machinery that takes over after proof exists

pros.claim: The founding-rate trade converts the operator's weakest moment into contractual proof assets
pros.example: five signed testimonial permissions existing before the fifth site even launched

cons.claim: Founding clients anchored on the low rate can resent the real price at renewal or referral time
cons.example: a founding client telling a referred friend the whole thing costs half of what the price sheet now says

failure_modes: hiding the discount's reason so early clients believe the founding rate is the price
spending the cold-start months polishing the offer instead of asking anyone to buy
acceptance_tests: each founding deal documents the disclosed time-boxed rate and holds signed testimonial and portfolio permission from day one
revisit_triggers: outreach replies show the fact-based opener reading as an insult or a scare in this niche
the founding cohort fills and the rate must sunset on schedule

base.update_signal: reply and close rates from the first outreach waves show which openers and channels the niche answers

nodes.definition: Assemble the proof kit that lets strangers buy: live client sites a prospect can visit, before-and-after screenshots used with written permission, named testimonials from recognizable local businesses, and claims that survive the verifiability test — a load-time comparison can be demonstrated on the spot, an uptime statement can come from monitoring records, while 'their revenue doubled' stays out unless the client documented it and approved saying so. Proof is deliberately niche-shaped: three finished plumber sites persuade the fourth plumber more than twenty generic portfolios, because the prospect recognizes the trade, the town, and the owner's name. The kit lives in the proposal, the outreach follow-up, and the one-page partner sheet, and every item in it carries its permission status so nothing shown was never cleared.

included: verifiability screening of every proof claim
excluded: the measurement infrastructure behind performance numbers
case-study claims the client never approved

pros.claim: Niche-recognizable proof collapses the trust gap that price talk cannot cross
pros.example: a prospect calling the roofer whose site is in the kit and hearing 'yes, he answers the phone' before signing

cons.claim: A permission-gated kit grows slowly and stays thin exactly when it is needed most
cons.example: two publishable sites in the kit while three finished clients decline to appear

failure_modes: showing work without permission and burning the referring client's trust
padding the kit with an unverifiable outcome claim that a sharp prospect dismantles in the meeting
acceptance_tests: every kit item carries permission status and every claim names its verification method or the client approval behind it
revisit_triggers: a launch produces a stronger, fresher proof piece than the current kit's oldest item
a client withdraws permission or leaves on bad terms

base.update_signal: prospect reactions show which proof pieces move deals and which sit unread

nodes.definition: Engineer referrals instead of waiting for them. The ask is timed to satisfaction peaks — launch day when the owner is proudly showing the site around, and the moment after a rescue (a same-day fix, a recovered domain) when gratitude is concrete — and it is made effortless: a single forwardable sentence plus the operator's card, not a request that the client compose a pitch. Any thank-you gesture or referral credit is disclosed to both sides so the referred prospect knows the introduction had a mechanism behind it. Every incoming lead is tagged with its source, which reveals which clients and partners actually feed the loop and which asks landed flat. The loop's fuel is delivered satisfaction — this node engineers the asking, while the sibling delivery and hosting knowledge earns the satisfaction being asked about.

excluded: the service quality that makes clients willing

pros.claim: Timed, effortless asks turn satisfied clients into a channel with near-zero acquisition cost
pros.example: a launch-day ask producing two plumber leads from the client's supplier group chat within a week

cons.claim: Referral dependence concentrates the pipeline in a few advocates whose silence starves it
cons.example: a quarter with no leads because the two best referrers had nothing new to mention

failure_modes: asking during a service complaint and converting mild dissatisfaction into voiced dissatisfaction
paying quiet referral bonuses that surface later and taint every past introduction
acceptance_tests: every incoming lead carries a source tag and every active thank-you arrangement is documented as disclosed
revisit_triggers: referral volume stays flat across two quarters
a lead reveals they never knew their introducer received a thank-you credit

base.update_signal: source-tagged lead data shows which asks, moments, and advocates actually produce clients

nodes.definition: Build referral partnerships with adjacent, non-competing professionals who sit in front of the niche's owners all year: the bookkeeper who sees every invoice, the print shop making the van decals, the sign maker, the trade supplier's counter staff, the chamber of commerce, and structured networking groups. Three arrangement classes exist — reciprocal referral (each sends the other fitting clients), a disclosed fee share on closed business, or plain goodwill — and whichever applies is written down and disclosed to referred clients per the selling rules. Each partner receives a one-page referral sheet stating who the offer is for, what it includes, and what it honestly does not do, so the partner describes the product accurately instead of promising rankings on the operator's behalf.

included: the three arrangement classes with disclosure
excluded: the client referral loop — that runs on delivered work, not partnerships

pros.claim: One well-placed partner multiplies reach across an entire niche's daily traffic
pros.example: a bookkeeper serving thirty local trades mentioning the offer whenever a client complains about their dead website

cons.claim: Partners paraphrase, and an unbriefed partner sells promises the offer refuses to make
cons.example: a well-meaning print-shop owner telling a customer the package 'gets you to the top of Google'

failure_modes: agreeing to a hidden fee share that violates the disclosure rule when it eventually surfaces
collecting many lukewarm partners instead of briefing the two who actually see the niche weekly
acceptance_tests: every active partner has a written arrangement class and holds the current referral sheet
revisit_triggers: a partner-referred prospect arrives with expectations the referral sheet does not support
a partner's referral volume or accuracy shifts notably

base.update_signal: source-tagged leads show which partner arrangements produce fitting clients and which produce mismatched expectations

nodes.definition: Run the small pipeline deliberately: every lead is logged with its source and next action, follow-up happens on a stated cadence instead of memory (an unanswered proposal gets its scheduled nudge, then a clean close-out message rather than eternal limbo), and intake respects capacity — when the month's build slots are spoken for, new deals are offered the next open slot with an honest start date instead of an overbooked promise. The cadence also reads the niche's seasons: trades sell best in their quiet planning months and want launches before their busy season, so outreach and start dates are planned against that rhythm. The pipeline's numbers — leads by source, close rate, slot utilization — are the feedback that re-scores the niche and re-times the outreach, not vanity counts.

included: stated follow-up cadence with clean close-outs
capacity-aware slotting with honest start dates
excluded: the build schedule itself — delivery territory

pros.claim: Capacity-aware intake protects launch dates, which protects the referral loop's fuel
pros.example: telling the fourth signer of the month their build starts on the first of next month — and hitting that date

cons.claim: Cadence discipline adds administrative weight a solo operator feels every single week
cons.example: an evening each Friday spent updating the lead log instead of building

failure_modes: accepting every signature in a hot month and blowing three launch dates at once
letting warm proposals rot because follow-up depended on remembering
acceptance_tests: the lead log shows source, next action, and outcome for every lead, and no accepted deal lacks a slot with a stated start date
revisit_triggers: slot utilization stays maxed or empty for a sustained stretch
the niche's seasonal pattern shifts from what the cadence assumed

base.update_signal: close-rate, slot-utilization, or seasonality data contradicts the cadence's assumptions

nodes.definition: Hold a structured discovery conversation before any quote, and let it disqualify. The call establishes: what the owner wants the site to cause (more calls, fewer wrong-address visits, credibility against a bigger rival), the current state — domain name, who registered it, who can access it, what exists today — content readiness (text and photos in hand, or nothing), whether the person talking can sign, budget-class fit against the package, and timeline reality. Explicit disqualifiers end the pursuit politely: needs beyond the package (multi-hundred-product commerce, custom portals), a demanded ranking or revenue guarantee that survives the honest explanation, no domain control and no willingness to recover it, or procurement behavior that predicts a nightmare client. The output is a recorded fit verdict with its reason; a disqualified prospect gets a straight answer and, where possible, a pointer to a better-fitting provider.

excluded: fixing the domain-access problem — delivery territory
pressure tactics to rescue a failing fit

pros.claim: Disqualifying early is the cheapest moment to lose a bad deal
pros.example: thirty minutes spent discovering a demanded ranking guarantee versus three months living under it

cons.claim: Rigid disqualification can eject a coachable prospect a second conversation would have landed
cons.example: a cafe owner who dropped the guarantee demand once the honest explanation actually reached her

failure_modes: quoting before discovering that nobody knows where the domain is registered
hearing the disqualifier and proceeding anyway because the month was slow
acceptance_tests: every quoted deal has a recorded discovery outcome covering goal, domain control, content readiness, decision-maker, and budget class, and every disqualification names its trigger
revisit_triggers: a signed client later reveals something discovery should have caught
the disqualifier list blocks a pattern of deals that in hindsight would have fit

base.update_signal: post-mortems on troubled clients show which discovery questions were missing or ignored

nodes.definition: Write the scope every deal signs before build work starts, as the contract's operational heart: the deliverables enumerated from the package sheet, the exclusions enumerated just as explicitly, the number of revision rounds and what one round means, the client's obligations — content items with due dates, feedback within stated windows, one consolidated voice for approvals — and the change-order path that prices any addition through a stated mechanism rather than a mood. The ownership and exit statement is referenced so it is signed, not just brochured. The scope's job is to make the fixed-price promise survivable: it is the document a polite refusal points to, the anchor a change order amends, and the reference that ends most disputes by being reread aloud.

excluded: jurisdiction-specific contract law — an obligation class for local verification
the build process the scope hands off to

pros.claim: A signed scope converts scope arguments from negotiations into document lookups
pros.example: settling the 'you said the blog was included' conversation by reading the exclusion line together

cons.claim: A scope written like a legal fortress can chill a trust-based local relationship
cons.example: a handshake-culture contractor balking at ten pages of defensive clauses for a five-page site

failure_modes: leaving revision rounds uncounted so 'one more tweak' never terminates
listing client content obligations without dates, making the stall clause unenforceable
acceptance_tests: the signed scope enumerates deliverables, exclusions, revision counts, dated client obligations, and the change-order path, and references the ownership statement
no build starts without the scope signed and the deposit received
revisit_triggers: a dispute arises the scope's wording could not settle
the package sheet is revised, forcing the scope template to follow

base.update_signal: a dispute, a template revision, or a change in the package sheet exposes a hole in the scope's wording

nodes.definition: Decide at scoping time who produces the words and pictures, because unassigned content is the single most common way a fixed-scope build dies. Three models, chosen and written per deal: client-provided — the client delivers listed items by listed dates, with a stall clause that pauses the project and re-slots it into a later build slot when dates lapse; done-for-you — copy and photo sourcing sold as a priced add-on with its own scope; or draft-first — the operator drafts every page from a short intake questionnaire and the client corrects rather than composes, which suits owners who freeze in front of a blank page. The chosen model, its dates, and its stall consequence go into the scope in plain words. How intake is mechanically run — forms, folders, checklists — belongs to the delivery process, not here; this node fixes accountability and its price.

included: dated obligations and the stall clause
pricing the done-for-you add-on by mechanism
excluded: intake tooling and checklists — delivery territory
writing fabricated claims into client copy
content strategy beyond the package's pages

pros.claim: The draft-first model removes the blank-page stall that kills client-provided content
pros.example: a mechanic answering twelve intake questions by phone and correcting a drafted services page in one sitting

cons.claim: Drafting for the client puts words in their mouth that may misstate the trade
cons.example: a drafted line implying emergency service the shop does not actually offer, caught only at review

failure_modes: signing a client-provided model with no dates and no stall clause, then owning the delay reputationally
quietly doing unpaid copywriting because the content never arrived and the launch date loomed
acceptance_tests: every signed scope names one of the three content models with dates and a stall consequence written in
revisit_triggers: stalls keep occurring under the model the niche was assumed to prefer
done-for-you requests exceed the capacity priced into the add-on

base.update_signal: stall frequency per content model shows which default the niche actually sustains

nodes.definition: Set expectations in writing at the moment they are cheapest to set — before work begins. The expectations document covers: the timeline with its client-dependency caveats made explicit (the launch date moves when content dates move, and here is how), what happens at launch and immediately after, what the care plan will and will not do month to month, the results honesty carried over from the capability line — the site will present the business properly and convert existing demand, and no traffic or ranking outcome is promised — and the communication contract: which channel, what response class, what counts as an emergency. It is walked through aloud, not merely attached, because expectations only bind when both sides heard the same sentence. This document is the referral loop's quiet engine: referrals come from clients whose expectations were met, and expectations can only be met if they were set.

included: the expectations document and its walkthrough
excluded: monthly reporting that later proves plan value — hosting-book territory

pros.claim: Explicitly moving the launch date with content dates turns delay blame into shared arithmetic
pros.example: a client conceding the slipped launch calmly because the walkthrough had traced exactly this chain

cons.claim: A heavy expectations ritual can feel bureaucratic to a two-page-site client
cons.example: a barber wondering why a simple site needs a meeting about communication channels

failure_modes: attaching the document unsigned and unread, then discovering each side remembers a different launch promise
promising a response class in the expectations document that contradicts the care-plan tier actually sold
acceptance_tests: every deal has an acknowledged expectations document whose timeline caveats, results honesty, and response class match the signed scope and plan tier
revisit_triggers: a client expresses surprise at something the document supposedly covered
the care-plan tiers or package timeline change upstream

base.update_signal: client-surprise incidents reveal which expectation the document failed to land

nodes.definition: Operate the discipline that keeps the fixed scope fixed once real clients start asking for 'one small thing'. Every out-of-scope request gets the same three-part treatment: acknowledged warmly (the request is legitimate, the timing is the question), logged to a visible parking lot so the client sees it is kept rather than dismissed, and routed — to a change order priced by the stated mechanism, to a named add-on, or to the post-launch edit allowance where it genuinely fits. Polite-refusal language is prepared in advance because improvised refusals collapse under friendliness. Goodwill is allowed but engineered: a small gesture is granted explicitly ('this one is on me — it is outside scope, but launch week deserves it'), never silently, because silent gifts are invisible and set precedent. Requests that cluster across clients flow back into the next package revision, turning creep pressure into product design signal.

excluded: hostile refusal that burns the relationship

pros.claim: The parking lot converts refusals into a post-launch sales list
pros.example: five parked requests becoming the client's first two change orders the month after launch

cons.claim: Rigid routing of trivial requests reads as nickel-and-diming
cons.example: invoicing a two-minute phone-number swap that goodwill should have absorbed

failure_modes: absorbing requests silently until the build runs at a loss and resentment leaks into the relationship
granting goodwill without labeling it, so the next free favor is expected
acceptance_tests: every out-of-scope request in the current book appears in a parking lot with its routing (change order, add-on, allowance, or labeled goodwill) recorded
revisit_triggers: the same request type is parked across three or more clients
goodwill grants for a single client accumulate past the bound the discipline set

base.update_signal: margin tracking or parking-lot patterns show creep leaking past the routing discipline

nodes.definition: Produce the proposal as the offer's condensed, signable form: one page a busy owner actually reads — the package named with its deliverable count, the build fee, the monthly plan with its tier, and the first-year total in one honest line — with the scope document and the ownership and exit statement attached as the substance behind the summary. Deposit mechanics are stated (what fraction starts the work, when the balance falls due) as mechanism, and the close is run without manufactured pressure: real capacity deadlines may be stated because they are true ('the next build slot opens on the first'), fake discounts and countdown timers may not, and a proposal that needs a scare to close is a proposal that failed discovery. The signature moment doubles as the checkpoint where disclosure obligations are met: the buyer can restate what they are buying, what it costs across the year, and how they would leave.

excluded: contract legalese drafting — an obligation class for local verification

pros.claim: A one-page proposal with the year's total up front closes on clarity instead of persuasion
pros.example: an owner signing at the kitchen table because everything fit on the page in front of the coffee

cons.claim: Radical simplicity can undersell the work's depth to a comparison shopper
cons.example: losing a bid to a rival's forty-page proposal that looked like more work was being bought

failure_modes: burying the monthly plan in fine print so the first renewal feels like a trap
reviving a stalled close with an invented expiring discount, violating the selling rules
acceptance_tests: the current proposal template shows both legs and the first-year total on page one with the ownership statement attached
a sampled recent close shows no undisclosed incentive and no fabricated deadline
revisit_triggers: proposals stall at the same section repeatedly
the price sheet, plan tiers, or ownership terms change upstream

base.update_signal: close-rate data or buyer questions show where the proposal confuses or conceals

nodes.definition: Gate every signed deal through a definition-of-sold checklist before it may enter the build queue, because a deal sold incompletely exports its chaos into delivery and hosting. The handoff packet must contain: the signed scope with its exclusions and revision counts, deposit received, the content model chosen with dated obligations, domain-control status verified during discovery (who holds it, and the recovery precondition if unresolved), the acknowledged expectations document, the care-plan tier recorded with its terms, and the testimonial and portfolio permissions collected at signing. The build process consumes this packet as its input contract, and the hosting book inherits the plan terms from it; a missing item bounces the deal back to the sales side to finish selling, and the sale is not counted as won until the packet is whole.

included: the bounce-back rule for incomplete sales
excluded: the build pipeline the packet feeds

pros.claim: A whole packet lets the build start without a single clarifying phone call
pros.example: a build week opening with content dates, plan tier, and domain status already answered on paper

cons.claim: A strict gate delays revenue recognition on deals that feel signed
cons.example: a deposit paid but the build slot held while the domain-control question limps toward an answer

failure_modes: starting a build on a signed-but-incomplete deal and rediscovering the missing domain access at launch week
letting the plan tier travel verbally so the hosting book onboards the client onto the wrong terms
acceptance_tests: no deal enters the build queue with an incomplete packet, and each packet item traces to its source document
revisit_triggers: delivery reports a recurring question the packet should have answered
the checklist grows stale against changes in the scope, plan, or permission templates

base.update_signal: delivery-side friction reports show which packet items are missing or ambiguous in practice

edges.why_related: the niche is chosen to give the productized package one coherent buyer
the honesty line is drawn around the specific promises the packaged offer makes
the ownership promise is a structural property of the offer, set when the offer is defined
the selling rules bind how the defined offer may be taken to market
the buyer profile is the chosen niche's signer, not a generic customer
the deliverable list is shaped by what the chosen niche's businesses need on a site
buyer fears and habits decide what belongs in the package and what stays an add-on
the plan is framed as custody of the specific site the package builds
the plan must be framed around the client's right to leave with their assets
the cost floor is computed from the package's actual deliverables and hours
the monthly price derives from what the framed plan promises to consume in cost and minutes
the economics model recomputes from the priced legs and their cost floors
cold-start outreach targets the counted local sample the niche choice produced
outreach openers must stay on the honest side of the capability line from the first message
the proof kit is assembled from founding clients' sites and their signed permissions
the forwardable ask leans on proof the referred prospect can immediately check
partners are picked for their daily contact with the chosen niche's owners
referral leads enter the same source-tagged log and cadence the pipeline runs on
partner-referred leads are tracked by source so each arrangement's yield is visible
discovery questions are phrased for the owner-operator the buyer profile describes
fit is judged against the package's enumerated deliverables and exclusions
the scope is written from discovery's recorded goal, content, and domain findings
the chosen content model and its stall clause are written into the scope's obligations
the expectations document restates the signed scope's timeline and obligations in client language
creep defense routes requests against the scope's enumerated lists and change path
the proposal quotes the versioned price sheet, never an improvised number
the proposal is the signable summary whose substance is the attached scope
the signature event immediately precedes assembling and checking the handoff packet
outreach may state observable facts about a broken site but never manufacture dread
every partner fee share must be disclosed to the referred client or refused
no proposal goes out without the ownership and exit statement attached
every proof claim must pass the verifiability test before it enters the kit
closing pressure tempts the pitch across the honesty line when a guarantee would win the signature
edges.resolution_rule: honesty wins: only verifiable commitments may be offered, and if the prospect's condition remains a ranking, traffic, or revenue guarantee, the deal is declined

edges.why_related: real prospects keep needing one thing the fixed package does not contain
edges.resolution_rule: package integrity wins: a genuine mismatch exits to a consciously priced custom quote or a referral out, and the package is never stretched silently for one deal

edges.why_related: the hunger for founding clients pushes early prices toward and below the floor
edges.resolution_rule: the cost floor holds: early discounts exist only as the disclosed, time-boxed founding rate traded for proof permissions, never as unbounded haggling room

edges.why_related: bundled custody naturally drifts toward stickiness that shades into lock-in
edges.resolution_rule: ownership wins: any plan structure that would make leaving with domain and content harder is restructured, and retention is earned by service quality alone

edges.why_related: expectations that were set and then met are what turn clients into willing referrers
the model's capacity and support-load math sets how many deals the cadence may accept per month
source-tagged conversion data re-scores the chosen niche against its scorecard over time
requests that cluster in the parking lot across clients become the next package revision's inputs

conflict_axes.name: fixed_package_vs_bespoke_demand
conflict_axes.description: The offer survives on repeatability, but nearly every prospect arrives with one special requirement the package does not contain, and each accommodation forks the product.
poles: keep the package a closed list
customize for each client's special need
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the package holds; a genuine mismatch exits to a consciously priced custom quote or a referral out, and clustered requests reshape the package only at its next versioned revision

conflict_axes.name: honest_claims_vs_closing_pressure
conflict_axes.description: Guarantee-shaped promises close deals, and the verifiability rule forbids exactly the promises prospects most want to hear.
poles: say only what can be verified
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the banned-claims list is absolute; the pitch redirects to verifiable commitments and walks away from deals conditioned on rankings, traffic, or revenue

conflict_axes.name: founding_rate_vs_price_integrity
conflict_axes.description: Early clients require a price concession the young business can barely justify, yet every concession teaches the market what the work costs.
poles: discount to win the cold start
hold the floor from day one
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: one disclosed, time-boxed founding rate traded for proof permissions, sunset on schedule; never an undisclosed discount that becomes the remembered price

conflict_axes.name: recurring_stickiness_vs_client_freedom
conflict_axes.description: The care plan's value comes from custody and continuity, which drifts naturally toward structures that make leaving painful — the exact lock-in the offer bans.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: portability is non-negotiable; stickiness may only be built from service quality, disclosed value, and the client's own preference to stay

conflict_axes.name: niche_focus_vs_opportunistic_revenue
conflict_axes.description: Off-niche leads with real budgets keep arriving, and each accepted one dilutes the proof kit, the referral density, and the repeatability the niche was chosen for.
poles: take good revenue wherever it appears
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: accept off-niche work only when the package fits unchanged; otherwise refer out, and re-aim the niche only on accumulated pipeline evidence, never on one deal

conflict_axes.name: goodwill_vs_scope_boundary
conflict_axes.description: Small favors preserve warm local relationships, but silent favors set precedents that dissolve the fixed scope one kindness at a time.
poles: grant favors to keep the relationship warm
route everything through the change-order gate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: goodwill is granted explicitly and labeled as outside scope, kept small and bounded; everything else routes to the change order or the parking lot

conflict_axes.name: pipeline_hunger_vs_qualification_rigor
conflict_axes.description: A dry month makes every disqualified prospect look salvageable, and rescued bad fits cost more in creep, disputes, and churn than the empty slot did.
poles: fill the slot with whoever will sign
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: a disqualification stands unless the disqualifying fact itself has changed; dry months trigger more outreach, not lower standards

conflict_axes.name: client_content_control_vs_launch_velocity
conflict_axes.description: Content the client insists on writing is content the launch waits for, and content the operator drafts risks putting wrong words in the business's mouth.
poles: wait for the client's authentic content
draft first and ship on schedule
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: choose the content model per deal at scoping with dates and a stall clause; default stalling clients toward draft-first, where the client corrects instead of composes

conflict_axes.name: build_fee_maximization_vs_recurring_base_growth
conflict_axes.description: Pricing energy gravitates to the visible one-time fee, but the business's compounding asset is the monthly base, and the two legs compete for the same buyer tolerance.
poles: price to grow the recurring base
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: both legs must clear their cost floors; when buyer tolerance forces a trade, protect the plan's price and margin because plans stack while build fees do not repeat

edge_cases.description: A prospect will only sign if the operator guarantees a first-page Google ranking
edge_cases.trigger: an outcome-guarantee demand survives the honest capability explanation at close
edge_cases.mitigation: restate what can honestly be promised — a fast, correct, credible site — offer only verifiable commitments, and decline the deal while leaving the door open

edge_cases.description: Discovery reveals the client's domain is registered under an unreachable ex-designer's personal account
edge_cases.trigger: the domain-control question surfaces a third-party registrant nobody can contact
edge_cases.mitigation: make domain recovery a written precondition in the scope with the timeline caveat attached, promise no launch date until control is confirmed, and hand the technical recovery to the delivery process

edge_cases.description: A prospect wants a five-hundred-product web shop inside the basic package
edge_cases.trigger: discovery surfaces needs that exceed the package's enumerated scope by an order of magnitude
edge_cases.mitigation: disqualify from the package honestly, then either refer out or offer a consciously priced custom project — never wedge commerce into the brochure package

edge_cases.description: A relative 'who does websites' appears after the proposal and undercuts the quote
edge_cases.trigger: a cheap informal competitor enters mid-negotiation
edge_cases.mitigation: hold the cost floor, restate custody, ownership, and verifiable proof as the difference, and let the deal go gracefully if price is the only axis — such clients often return after the relative disappears

edge_cases.description: A client pays the deposit and then goes silent on content for six weeks
edge_cases.trigger: content due dates lapse with no deliverables and no responses
edge_cases.mitigation: run the written stall clause: the scheduled nudges, then a pause-and-re-slot notice, with the done-for-you add-on or draft-first switch offered as the path back

edge_cases.description: An elderly shop owner is ready to sign without grasping that the plan renews monthly
edge_cases.trigger: the buyer's questions reveal confusion about recurring billing at the close
edge_cases.mitigation: slow the close, restate the first-year total in plain words, invite a family member or the bookkeeper into the decision, and honor any cooling-off obligation class in the jurisdiction

edge_cases.description: A bookkeeper offers steady referrals but wants the fee share kept secret from referred clients
edge_cases.trigger: a partner conditions the channel on an undisclosed kickback
edge_cases.mitigation: decline the undisclosed arrangement and counter-offer a disclosed thank-you or reciprocal referrals; a channel bought with hidden fees poisons every introduction it makes

edge_cases.description: A twice-burned prospect insists on holding the hosting account themselves and doubts the plan's honesty
edge_cases.trigger: past vendor hostage-holding makes bundled custody itself the objection
edge_cases.mitigation: show the written exit terms, put the domain in their name immediately, and accept a build-only deal if custody trust is not yet earned — the plan can be sold later on demonstrated service

edge_cases.description: A strong referral arrives from a business outside the chosen niche
edge_cases.trigger: an off-niche lead with real budget lands via a trusted referrer
edge_cases.mitigation: accept only if the package fits unchanged; otherwise refer out with thanks, log the lead's source, and treat one deal as data, not as a reason to re-aim the offer

edge_cases.description: A client asks the operator to write 'best plumber in the county' and to invent review quotes for the site
edge_cases.trigger: fabricated or unverifiable claims are requested for site copy during scoping
edge_cases.mitigation: refuse invented reviews outright, and replace superlatives with verifiable facts — license classes held, years operating, real testimonials with written permission

edge_cases.description: A prospect wants the monthly price lowered by dropping backups from the plan
edge_cases.trigger: unbundling of the plan's protective core is proposed at the close
edge_cases.mitigation: keep hosting, updates, and backups unsplittable; offer a smaller edit allowance or a leaner tier instead, and decline the deal rather than custody a site with no backups

edge_cases.description: Three builds sign in the same month and exceed the solo operator's capacity
edge_cases.trigger: signed work outruns the monthly build slots
edge_cases.mitigation: slot deals with disclosed start dates at proposal time, waitlist honestly instead of overpromising, and use the capacity math — not panic — to decide whether subcontracting is worth its margin and quality risk

workflow.description: Fix the package as the unit of sale with a build leg and a recurring care leg, aimed at one kind of buyer
workflow.gate: the deliverable set, both revenue legs, and the target buyer are stated on one page and read back identically by two outside readers

workflow.description: Run the five-criterion scorecard against counted local samples and commit to one niche
workflow.artifact: niche scorecard with the chosen niche and its counted sample
workflow.gate: the chosen niche passes ability-to-pay, urgency, content-simplicity, referral-density, and low-custom-demand checks

workflow.description: Write the can/cannot capability sheet and the banned-claims list every sales artifact must obey
workflow.artifact: capability claims sheet with banned-claims list
workflow.gate: every allowed claim names its verification method and ranking/traffic/revenue guarantees sit on the banned list

workflow.description: Write the disclosure-first, no-fear-selling, vulnerable-buyer, and incentive-disclosure rules that bind all acquisition
workflow.gate: every outreach template and the proposal template in use pass the rules on review

workflow.action: Write the ownership and exit promise
workflow.description: Fix domain, content, and deliverable ownership terms and the written exit path before anything is sold
workflow.gate: domain arrangement, content ownership, and the handover path are stated and attached to the proposal template

workflow.description: Enumerate deliverables, exclusions, revision counts, and named add-ons as closed lists
workflow.gate: a reader can classify any plausible request as included, add-on, or excluded without asking

workflow.action: Frame the care plan and price both legs
workflow.description: State the plan's sold promise, then derive the build fee and monthly price from the documented cost floor with margin
workflow.artifact: cost-floor worksheet and versioned price sheet
workflow.gate: both prices clear the documented floor by the stated margin and no sales artifact asserts an invented market figure

workflow.description: Work warm paths and fact-based outreach into the niche under the disclosed founding-rate arrangement
workflow.artifact: founding-client roster with disclosed terms and signed permissions
workflow.gate: each founding deal documents the time-boxed rate and holds testimonial and portfolio permission from signing

workflow.description: Build the niche-shaped proof kit from founding sites, permissioned material, and verifiable claims
workflow.gate: every item carries permission status and every claim passes the verifiability test

workflow.action: Run discovery and qualify every lead
workflow.description: Hold the structured discovery call, probe domain control and content readiness, and record a fit verdict
workflow.gate: goal, domain control, content readiness, budget class, and decision-maker are recorded and the disqualifier list was applied

workflow.action: Write the scope and close without pressure
workflow.description: Turn discovery findings into the signed scope and the one-page proposal with the first-year total disclosed
workflow.gate: deliverables, exclusions, revision counts, dated client obligations, the change-order path, and the ownership statement are signed together

workflow.description: Assemble the handoff packet and hold the deal at the definition-of-sold gate until it is whole
workflow.gate: scope, deposit, content model with dates, domain-control status, acknowledged expectations, plan tier, and permissions are all present

dominance_rules.rule: When any retention or bundling idea conflicts with the client's ownership of domain and content, ownership wins
dominance_rules.rationale: lock-in through hostage-holding destroys trust, referrals, and possibly legal standing; this business retains through service quality
dominance_rules.trigger: a plan structure, contract clause, or registrar choice would make leaving harder
dominance_rules.action: restructure so the client can leave with domain and content intact, then compete on service

dominance_rules.rule: When closing pressure conflicts with honest capability claims, honesty wins
dominance_rules.rationale: one guaranteed-ranking promise creates an unpayable debt that ends in dispute and reputation damage
dominance_rules.trigger: a prospect conditions signing on a traffic, ranking, or revenue outcome
dominance_rules.action: offer only verifiable commitments and decline the deal if the guarantee remains the condition

dominance_rules.rule: Ethical-selling guardrails dominate every acquisition tactic
dominance_rules.rationale: fear-selling and hidden incentives convert once and then destroy the local reputation the whole model runs on
dominance_rules.trigger: an outreach script, audit framing, or partner arrangement leans on dread or undisclosed fees
dominance_rules.action: rewrite the tactic to disclosure-first framing or drop it entirely

dominance_rules.rule: The written scope dominates verbal goodwill
dominance_rules.rationale: unwritten promises are remembered differently by each side and compound into free work and resentment
dominance_rules.trigger: a client cites a hallway promise absent from the signed scope
dominance_rules.action: route the request through the change-order path and grant only explicit, labeled, bounded goodwill

dominance_rules.rule: The documented cost floor dominates competitive undercutting
dominance_rules.rationale: a below-floor deal loses money on every month it lives and teaches the market a false price
dominance_rules.trigger: a cheaper competitor or a client's relative undercuts a live proposal
dominance_rules.action: hold the floor, restate custody and verifiable proof, and let the deal go if price is the only axis

dominance_rules.rationale: a rescued bad fit costs more in creep, disputes, and churn than the empty build slot ever did
dominance_rules.trigger: a dry month tempts the operator to reopen a disqualified deal
dominance_rules.action: keep the disqualification unless the disqualifying fact itself has changed; answer dry months with more outreach

dominance_rules.rationale: every silent exception forks the product, breaks the pricing floor's assumptions, and unravels repeatability
dominance_rules.trigger: a prospect's needs exceed the package during discovery or scoping
dominance_rules.action: exit to a consciously priced custom quote or refer out; never stretch the package silently

dominance_rules.rationale: overbooked builds slip, break set expectations, and stall the referral loop at its source
dominance_rules.trigger: signed or imminent deals exceed the month's build slots
dominance_rules.action: offer disclosed later start dates or an honest waitlist instead of an overpromise

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the niche before designing the package
anti_rework_rules.prevents: rebuilding the package, proof kit, and outreach for a different buyer after mis-aimed early sales

anti_rework_rules.rule: Enumerate the package's exclusions before the first sales conversation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: mid-build disputes over what the fee included and the goodwill free work used to settle them

anti_rework_rules.rule: Document the cost floor before publishing or quoting any price
anti_rework_rules.prevents: repricing the entire client book after discovering every plan quietly loses money

anti_rework_rules.rule: Verify domain control and fix the content responsibility model during discovery, before any timeline promise
anti_rework_rules.prevents: stalled builds, blown launch dates, and blame when a domain or the copy never arrives

anti_rework_rules.rule: Attach the ownership and exit statement to the proposal template before the first proposal goes out
anti_rework_rules.prevents: renegotiating trust deal-by-deal and inconsistent promises surfacing at client exits

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix revision-round counts in the scope before design work starts
anti_rework_rules.prevents: the infinite polish loop that consumes a fixed fee one 'small tweak' at a time

anti_rework_rules.rule: Collect testimonial and portfolio permission at signing, not after launch
anti_rework_rules.prevents: months of chasing proof and a kit padded with unusable anonymous claims

anti_rework_rules.rule: Define the change-order path before the first out-of-scope request arrives
anti_rework_rules.prevents: improvised free favors hardening into the precedent every later request cites

iteration_protocol.trigger: two consecutive prospects in the niche disqualify on budget class
iteration_protocol.action: re-score the niche's ability to pay and re-derive both prices from the cost floor before further outreach

iteration_protocol.trigger: the same change-order request appears across three or more clients
iteration_protocol.action: fold the request into the next versioned package revision or a named add-on

iteration_protocol.trigger: tool or hosting cost rises push the plan's margin below the stated floor
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the cost-floor worksheet, version the price sheet for new deals, and apply increase mechanics to existing clients per their terms

iteration_protocol.trigger: referral volume stays flat for two quarters
iteration_protocol.action: audit ask timing, proof freshness, and whether launch expectations were actually met

iteration_protocol.trigger: proposals repeatedly lose to cheaper informal competitors
iteration_protocol.action: strengthen verifiable proof and custody framing in the proposal rather than cutting below the floor

iteration_protocol.trigger: a departing client reports friction reclaiming their domain or content
iteration_protocol.action: repair the exit path immediately and restate the ownership terms in the proposal template

iteration_protocol.trigger: signed builds exceed monthly capacity for a sustained stretch
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the capacity math and adjust intake pacing, waitlist terms, or the subcontracting decision

priority_rationale: The frame nodes (offer thesis, niche, buyer reality) come first because the package, its honesty rails, and its ownership promise are all designed against one chosen buyer; offer design (package, care-plan framing, cost-floor pricing, economics) must be fixed before acquisition so the founding clients buy the real product at a survivable price; acquisition (founding clients, proof, referrals, partners, cadence) feeds discovery; and the scoping chain (qualification, scope, content split, expectations, creep defense) precedes the close and the definition-of-sold handoff because every downstream dispute is cheapest to prevent at the moment the scope is written.
